claims.claim: In 1726 Mary Toft convinced the king's surgeon she was giving birth to rabbits
claims.quote: He delivered several pieces of animal flesh and duly notified other prominent physicians, which brought the case to the attention of Nathaniel St. André, surgeon to the Royal Household of King George I. St. André concluded that Toft's case was genuine

claims.claim: Mary Toft was from Godalming, Surrey
claims.quote: was an English woman from Godalming, Surrey, who in 1726 became the subject of considerable controversy when she tricked doctors into believing that she had given birth to rabbits.

claims.claim: The portrait was made while she was in prison
claims.quote: By this time she had become quite ill, and while incarcerated had her portrait drawn by John Laguerre.

claims.claim: The portrait is by John Laguerre, 1726
claims.quote:
Description: A copy of a portrait of Mary Toft
Date: 1726
Author: John Laguerre

claims.claim: She said a rabbit startled her in a field
claims.quote: They had also invented a story in which Toft claimed that during her pregnancy and while working in a field, she had been startled by a rabbit, and had since become obsessed with rabbits.

claims.claim: She was working while pregnant, chased the rabbit and failed to catch it
claims.quote: being working in a Field with other Women, they put up a Rabbit, who running from them, they pursued it, but to no Purpose

claims.claim: She then miscarried and said she could think of nothing else
claims.quote: This created in her such a Longing to it, that she (being with Child) was taken ill and miscarried, and from that Time she hath not been able to avoid thinking of Rabbits.

claims.claim: The broadsheet 'The Doctors in Labour' dates from 1726
claims.quote:
Archive title: File:Mary toft the doctors in labour.jpg
Description: Doctors in Labour, or a new whim-wham from Guildford. ... Date: 1726

claims.claim: A surgeon wrote that the twelfth rabbit was 'now leaping'
claims.quote: As soon as the eleventh Rabbet was taken away, up leap'd the twelfth Rabbet, which is now leaping.

claims.claim: John Howard invited anyone who doubted the story to come and watch a delivery
claims.quote: Howard had Toft moved to Guildford, where he offered to deliver rabbits in the presence of anyone who doubted her story.

claims.claim: Henry Davenant of the royal court came to see the case and believed it
claims.quote: on 4 November Henry Davenant, a member of the court of King George I, went to see for himself what was happening.  He examined the samples Howard had collected and returned to London, ostensibly a believer.

claims.claim: Hogarth's 'Cunicularii, or The Wise Men of Godliman' dates from 1726
claims.quote: William Hogarth published Cunicularii, or The Wise Men of Godliman in Consultation (1726)

claims.claim: The royal surgeon concluded the rabbits bred in her fallopian tubes
claims.quote: St. André then performed a medical examination on Toft, and concluded that the rabbits were bred in her fallopian tubes.

claims.claim: St André tested a piece of rabbit lung in water to see if it had breathed
claims.quote: To check if it had breathed air, he placed a piece of its lung in water to see if it would float—which it did.

claims.claim: He staked his reputation on a 40-page pamphlet
claims.quote: who on 3 December had published his forty-page pamphlet A Short Narrative of an Extraordinary Delivery of Rabbets. On this document the surgeon had staked his reputation

claims.claim: The engraving of Mary Toft is by James Caulfield, 1819
claims.quote:
Date: 1819
Author: James Caulfield (1764–1826)

claims.claim: Ahlers found cut marks, and straw and grain in the droppings
claims.quote: Upon closer study, he reportedly found evidence of them having been cut with a man-made instrument, and noted pieces of straw and grain in their droppings.

claims.claim: Surgeon Cyriacus Ahlers took specimens away with him
claims.quote: before making his excuses and returning to London, taking specimens of the rabbits with him

claims.claim: The etching is by John Clark, c.1726
claims.quote:

claims.claim: She confessed that the parts had been inserted into her body
claims.quote: Following her miscarriage and while her cervix permitted access, an accomplice had inserted into her womb the claws and body of a cat, and the head of a rabbit.

claims.claim: She was discharged in 1727 because nobody knew what to charge her with
claims.quote: She was ultimately discharged on 8 April 1727, as it was unclear as to what charge should have been made against her.

claims.claim: Who devised the plot was never settled / remains unresolved
claims.quote: In her earlier, unpublished confessions, she blamed the entire affair on a range of other participants, from her mother-in-law to John Howard.

claims.claim: Hogarth's 'Credulity, Superstition and Fanaticism' dates from 1762
claims.quote: Author: William Hogarth ... Date: 1762-04

claims.claim: She confessed on 7 December 1726
claims.quote: After several days of this Manningham threatened to perform a painful operation on her, and on 7 December, in the presence of Manningham, Douglas, John Montagu and Frederick Calvert, Toft finally confessed.

claims.claim: Toft was a 24-year-old field worker from Godalming, Surrey
claims.quote: The 'poor Woman', Mary Toft, was twenty-four or twenty-five years old.

claims.claim: In 1726 she became pregnant and miscarried
claims.quote: In 1726 Toft became pregnant, but following her reported fascination with the sighting of a rabbit, she miscarried.

claims.claim: Local man-midwife John Howard delivered what he described as rabbits
claims.quote: Ann Toft sent the flesh to John Howard, a Guildford-based man-midwife of thirty years' experience.

claims.claim: King George I sent Nathaniel St André, surgeon to the Royal Household, who examined her
claims.quote: By the middle of November the British royal family were so interested in the story that they sent St. André and Samuel Molyneux, secretary to the Prince of Wales, to investigate.

claims.claim: St André published his pamphlet on 3 December, four days before her confession
claims.quote: who on 3 December had published his forty-page pamphlet A Short Narrative of an Extraordinary Delivery of Rabbets

claims.claim: A porter at the bagnio admitted he had been bribed to smuggle a rabbit into her chamber
claims.quote: Thomas Howard, a porter at the bagnio, confessed to Justice of the Peace Sir Thomas Clarges that he had been bribed by Toft's sister-in-law, Margaret, to sneak a rabbit into Toft's chamber.

claims.claim: The inserted parts included cat claws and a rabbit's head
claims.quote: an accomplice had inserted into her womb the claws and body of a cat, and the head of a rabbit

claims.claim: She was jailed as a 'vile cheat and impostor'
claims.quote: before being sent to Tothill Fields Bridewell, charged on a statute of Edward III as a "vile cheat and impostor"

claims.claim: Howard was fined £800
claims.quote: On 7 January 1727 John Howard and Mary Toft appeared before the bench, where Howard was fined £800 (£141,023 today).

claims.claim: St André's career never recovered
claims.quote: but the careers of St. André and his wife were permanently damaged

claims.claim: Her unpublished confessions blamed her mother-in-law, Howard, and a travelling woman who said the scheme would mean she'd 'never want as long as I liv'd'
claims.quote: In her earlier, unpublished confessions, she blamed the entire affair on a range of other participants, from her mother-in-law to John Howard. She also claimed that a travelling woman told her how to insert the rabbits into her body, and how such a scheme would ensure that she would "never want as long as I liv'd".

claims.claim: Her sister-in-law Margaret refused to say anything at all
claims.quote:
Margaret, under Douglas's interrogation, claimed that she had obtained the rabbit for eating only.

I told my sister of my having sent for a rabbit and I desire[d] her to give it to the porter to be carryed away
